If a function can be reversed, then its derivative tells us the derivative of the reverse function. The two slopes are reciprocals, but at corresponding points.

exercise.title: Why are inverse slopes reciprocals at matching points?

statement.p: If b=f(a) and f'(a)=4, then a small input change produces about four times as much output change, so the inverse slope at b is 1/4. In your own words, why must we use the original slope at a rather than at b, and why is a formula for f^{-1} unnecessary?

hint.p: Inverse functions swap the roles of input and output. The matching point is the pair (a,b), reflected across y=x.

subsection.title: Why the nonzero derivative matters
subsection.p: This condition is not decorative. If the original graph has a horizontal tangent, then the inverse graph has a vertical tangent. A vertical tangent does not have a finite derivative as a function of x.

exercise.title: Why does a horizontal tangent block a finite inverse derivative?

statement.p: The cube function is strictly increasing, so it has an inverse, but f'(0)=0 and \sqrt[3]{x} has a vertical tangent at the origin. In your own words, why can an inverse exist while the inverse derivative formula cannot be used?

hint.p: Reflection across y=x turns a horizontal tangent into a vertical tangent. A vertical tangent has no finite slope as a function of x.

exercise.title: Why must sine be restricted before it has an inverse?

statement.p: Many angles share the same sine value, so sine is not one-to-one on the whole line. In your own words, why does choosing the interval [-\pi/2,\pi/2] make \arcsin x well-defined, and why is \sin^{-1}x a dangerous notation?

hint.p: An inverse needs a unique output for each input in the range. The notation \sin^{-1}x is easily confused with a reciprocal.

warning.title: Notation warning

exercise.title: Why do \arcsin and \arctan produce those algebraic derivatives?

statement.p: Implicit differentiation of \sin y=x produces a cosine in the denominator, which is then rewritten as \sqrt{1-x^2}. In your own words, why is the square root nonnegative, why are the endpoint derivatives infinite, and why is 1/(1+x^2) the fingerprint of arctangent?

hint.p: On the chosen range, cosine does not change sign. The graph of \arcsin x becomes vertical at x=\pm 1, while \arctan x is differentiable for every real input.

Inverse functions reverse input and output. The next section returns to powers, where the exponent need not be an integer. That extension also depends on reversing functions, because real powers are most naturally handled with logarithms.
